references.text: The Pool of Siloam is mentioned in [ref:Joh 9:7-11|John 9:7-11], providing geographical context to the Tower of Siloam that Jesus refers to in Luke 13:4.
[ref:Luk 13:1-3|Luke 13:1-3] is the immediate context where Jesus uses the example of the Galileans whom Pilate killed, and raises the same question about guilt and repentance as in verse 4.
[ref:Luk 13:5|Luke 13:5] is Jesus' conclusion after the example of the Tower of Siloam: without repentance, all will perish in the same way.

Job's friends claimed that misfortune strikes the guilty: "Who perished without guilt?" ([ref:Job 4:7|Job 4:7]). Jesus rejects this line of thinking by showing that the victims of the Tower of Siloam were not greater sinners than others.

[ref:Esek 18:1-4|Ezekiel 18:1-4] addresses the question of individual guilt and God's justice – the same theme Jesus touches on when he rejects the idea that the victims of misfortune were more guilty than others.
[ref:Luk 12:57-59|Luke 12:57-59] is about settling your account in time, which thematically connects with Jesus' call to repentance in Luke 13:1-5.

In [ref:Joh 9:1-3|John 9:1-3], Jesus rejects the idea that the suffering of the man born blind was due to personal sin – the same principle as in Luke 13:4, where Jesus denies that the victims of the disaster were greater sinners than others.

[ref:Rom 2:4-5|Romans 2:4-5] emphasizes that God's kindness is meant to lead to repentance, and that those who do not repent store up wrath – parallel to Jesus' warning that all will perish without repentance.
[ref:2 Pet 3:9|2 Peter 3:9] says that the Lord is patient and wants all to come to repentance, a theme underlying Jesus' exhortation in Luke 13:4-5.
